* *

And His saying: ﴿And He is the Exalted in Might﴾

He means: He is the Strong, whose punishment of those who disobey Him and oppose His command is severe. ﴿the Forgiving﴾ means: the Forgiver of the sins of those who turn to Him in repentance and repent of their sins.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 67, verses 3–4:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Who created seven heavens in layers. You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful. So return your gaze; do you see any rifts? (3) Then return your gaze twice; your gaze will return to you humbled, while it is weary.﴾ (4)

His, may He be exalted and remembered, says, informing about His attribute: ﴿Who created seven heavens in layers﴾, layer upon layer, one above another.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾

He, may His praise be great, says: You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful, which He created, neither in the heaven nor in the earth, nor in anything else, any discrepancy, meaning any difference.

The people of interpretation have said what is similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾: you do not see among them any difference.

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿discrepancy﴾, he said: difference.

The reciters differed in the reading of this. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra, and some of the Kufans, read ﴿tafawut﴾ with an alif. The majority of the reciters of Kufa read ﴿tafawwut﴾ with a doubled waw and without an alif.

The correct view on this is that they are two well-known readings with one meaning, just as it is said: "wa la tusa'ir" and "wa la tusa''ir" (do not turn your cheek); and "ta'ahhadtu fulanan" and "ta'ahadtuhu" (I attended to someone); and "tazahhartu" and "tazahartu" (I backed up); and likewise al-tafawut and al-tafawwut.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿So return your gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾

He says: Return the gaze; do you see in it any splits? It is from the saying of God: ﴿The heavens are nearly torn apart from above them﴾, meaning they crack and split. Al-futur is the verbal noun of futira, futuran.

The people of interpretation have said what is similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿do you see any rifts?﴾: he said: the futur is the weakness (al-wahy).

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿do you see any rifts?﴾: he says: do you see any flaw, O son of Adam.

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿any rifts﴾: he said: any flaw.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, regarding ﴿do you see any rifts?﴾: he said: any cracks.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾

He, may His praise be great, says: Then return your gaze, O son of Adam, twice, one time after another, and look: ﴿do you see any rifts?﴾ or discrepancy. ﴿Your gaze will return to you humbled﴾ means: your gaze will return to you in humiliation, expelled, from their saying to the dog "ukhsa'", when they drive it away, meaning it is driven away humbled. ﴿While it is weary﴾ means: while it is exhausted and fatigued.

The people of interpretation have said what is similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾: he says: do you see any gap in the sky? ﴿Your gaze will return to you humbled while it is weary﴾: by the darkness of the night.

Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿humbled while it is weary﴾: he says: humiliated; and His saying: ﴿while it is weary﴾: he says: trembling.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿Your gaze will return to you humbled﴾, meaning: dazzled, ﴿while it is weary﴾, meaning: exhausted.

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿humbled﴾: he said: lowly; ﴿while it is weary﴾: he says: exhausted, having seen no gap or discrepancy.

Some of them said: al-khasi'** and al-hasir are one and the same.

Those who said that:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: (So return your gaze; do you see any rifts?) ... the verse, he said: al-khasi' and al-khasir are one; his sight was exhausted from seeing any splitting in it, so it returned while weary before seeing any splitting in it. He said: when the Day of Resurrection comes, it will split, then it will be torn apart, then a greater matter than that will come, and it will be uncovered.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 67, verses 5–7:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and made them missiles against the devils, and prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾ (5)

His, the Exalted's, saying means: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾, which are the stars, and We made them lamps because of their light. Likewise, the dawn (subh) is so called only because of the light that shines for people from the day. ﴿And made them missiles against the devils﴾ means: and We made the lamps with which We adorned the nearest heaven into missiles by which the devils are stoned.

And Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾: Indeed, Allah, His praise be exalted, created these stars for three purposes: He created them as an adornment for the nearest heaven, as missiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided. Whoever interprets them otherwise has spoken by his own opinion, has erred in his share, has wasted his portion, and has burdened himself with what he has no knowledge of.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾

His, the Exalted's, saying means: And We have prepared for the devils, in the Hereafter, the punishment of the Blaze, in which they will be kindled and set ablaze.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination. (6) When they are cast into it, they will hear from it a roaring, while it boils up (7)﴾

His, the Exalted's, saying means: ﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾, who created them in the world, ﴿is the punishment of Hell﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾. He means: and wretched is the destination, the punishment of Hell.

* *

His saying: ﴿When they are cast into it﴾

means: when the disbelievers are cast into Hell. ﴿They will hear from it﴾, meaning from Hell, ﴿a roaring (shahiq)﴾. By shahiq is meant the sound that comes out from the chest with intensity, like the braying of a donkey, as Ru'bah said in describing a donkey:

He chokes in his throat a hoarse sound, or a roar, until it is said he brays, though he has not brayed.

[[The two verses are in (Diwan of Ru'bah al-Rajiz, Leipzig edition, p. 106). Hashraja al-himar: he cut off his voice and repeated it in his throat. Al-sahil: a sound tending toward hoarseness that circulates in the donkey's chest; likewise al-sahal with a dammah. Al-shahiq: the braying of a donkey. Al-shahiq: drawing in breath; al-zafir: expelling breath. God, mighty and majestic, said regarding the people of the Fire: (For them therein is zafir and shahiq). Al-Zajjaj said: al-zafir and al-shahiq are among the sounds of those in distress. He said: al-zafir is from the intense groan and its ugliness; al-shahiq is the very high, intense groan. He said: Some lexicographers of Basra and Kufa claimed that al-zafir is like the beginning of a donkey's bray, and al-shahiq is like the end of its sound in the shahiq. It was narrated from al-Rabi' regarding His saying: (For them therein is zafir and shahiq) that he said: the zafir is in the throat, and the shahiq is in the chest (Lisan al-Arab: sh-h-q).]]

* *

His saying: ﴿while it boils up﴾

He says: it seethes.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿they will hear from it a roaring while it boils up﴾: it seethes as a cooking pot seethes.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 67, verse 22:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Is one who walks prone on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Is one who walks﴾ O people ﴿prone on his face﴾, not seeing what is before him, nor what is to his right or left, ﴿better guided﴾, meaning more upright on the road and better guided by it, ﴿or one who walks upright﴾, the walking of the children of Adam on their feet, ﴿on a straight path﴾, meaning: on a road with no crookedness in it.

It is said that ﴿mukibban﴾ (prone) is used because the verb is intransitive (ghayr waqi'); when it is not transitive they add the alif, saying: akabba fulan 'ala wajhihi, fa-huwa mukibb ("so-and-so fell prone on his face, and he is mukibb"). From this is the verse of al-A'sha:

Mukibban 'ala rawqayhi yahfiru 'irqaha / 'ala zahri 'uryan al-tariqati ahyama

[The verse is by al-A'sha of Banu Qays ibn Tha'laba (his Diwan, p. 295), from a qasida in praise of Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta'i, and the verse describes a wild bull, to which a she-camel is likened. Mukibban: lowering its head. Yahfiru al-artah (in the verse before it): digging the shrub to make a burrow in which to shelter. Rawqayhi: his two horns. 'Ala zahri 'uryan al-tariqati: on the surface of the exposed road. Ahyam: crumbling, not holding together, and it describes ('uryan al-tariqati). He says: the bull lowered itself over the root of the tree with its horns, digging in it a den to shelter in, in this exposed place whose sand crumbles without holding together. The author cited the verse as evidence for the saying of God, the Exalted: "Is one who walks prone on his face" meaning lowering himself towards the ground. Al-Farra' said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 338): "His saying: 'Is one who walks prone on his face'. You say: qad akabba al-rajulu when the action did not pass to an object (intransitive); when the action passes (transitive), you drop the alif, so you say: qad kabbahu Allah li-wajhihi, and kabbtuhu ana li-wajhihi." End quote.]

He said: mukibban, because the verb is intransitive; when it is transitive, the alif is removed, so it is said: kabbabtu fulanan 'ala wajhihi, and kabbahu Allah 'ala wajhihi.

The people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said.

The correct reading in this matter is that which the reciters of the metropolitan cities hold, due to the consensus of the authoritative reciters upon it.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should sink away into the earth, who would bring you flowing water?﴾ (67:30)**

Exalted is He, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to these polytheists: ﴿Have you considered﴾, O people who set up equals with God, ﴿if your water should sink away﴾, meaning, become sunken, out of reach of buckets, ﴿who would bring you flowing water﴾, meaning, who would bring you flowing water? By "flowing" (mu'in) he means water that is visible to the eyes on the surface.

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) have said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿who would bring you flowing water﴾, he said: "Sweet water."

Ibn Abd al-A'la ibn Wasil narrated to us, saying: Ubayd ibn Qasim al-Bazzaz narrated to me, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Salim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His words: ﴿if your water should sink away﴾, "out of reach of buckets" ﴿who would bring you flowing water﴾, he said: "The apparent (visible) water."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should sink away﴾, he said: "That is, gone away." ﴿who would bring you flowing water﴾, he said: "Flowing water (al-ma' al-mu'in) is running water."

It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His words: ﴿your water sink away﴾, "gone away." ﴿who would bring you flowing water﴾, "running."

It is said that ghawran (sunken) is used here as a description of water with a verbal noun (masdar), as one says "laylah 'amm" (a general night), meaning "a general/widespread night."
